templates.name: Main purpose: literary reaction, mood or trait
Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Three moves: introduces a project, details its approach, gives a critique it received
Three moves: explains a finding, generalizes it to a pattern, explains an exception
Main purpose: profile of a person, work or institution
Function: qualification of an earlier description
The speaker describes attempts or efforts, then acknowledges a limit (poem)
Describes a common view, then a recent finding that challenges it

items.passage: Tawny crazy ants (Nylanderia fulva), which reached the southern United States from South America, frequently displace imported fire ants (Solenopsis invicta), another South American invader notorious for its venomous sting. Investigating this displacement, Edward LeBrun, Nathan Jones, and Lawrence Gilbert observed that after exposure to fire ant venom, a crazy ant applies secretions from an abdominal gland to its exoskeleton. Laboratory bioassays demonstrated that formic acid in these secretions detoxifies the venom, a capability that, the researchers propose, probably contributes substantially to the crazy ants’ competitive success.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes a chemical defense used by one invasive ant species in order to argue that the species should be controlled before it spreads any farther.
It summarizes research that identifies a defensive behavior in one invasive ant species and suggests how it may help that species prevail over another.
It reports how one invasive ant protects itself from a rival’s venom in order to show that the venom is less dangerous to other insects than scientists had believed.
It summarizes research identifying a chemical made by one invasive ant species and explaining how that chemical allows the species to locate its rivals’ nests.
items.explanation: The text first notes that tawny crazy ants often displace fire ants, then describes what LeBrun and his colleagues observed (crazy ants smear a gland secretion over themselves after exposure to fire ant venom), then reports that formic acid in the secretion detoxifies the venom, which the researchers think probably helps explain the crazy ants’ success. Choice B states both parts of this purpose: the research identifies a defensive behavior and suggests how it may help one invader prevail over another.

A.why_wrong: The text does describe a chemical defense in an invasive ant, but it only reports the research; it never recommends controlling the species or warns about its spread.

C.why_wrong: The text does describe a crazy ant protecting itself from fire ant venom, but it says nothing about the venom’s effect on other insects or about what scientists had believed; the detox behavior is presented as the crazy ant’s own competitive advantage.

D.recipe: first part true, later link invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The research does identify a chemical the crazy ants make (formic acid), but the text says it detoxifies fire ant venom, not that it helps the ants find their rivals’ nests.

sources.what: LeBrun, Jones, Gilbert (Science 2014): after exposure to fire ant venom, tawny crazy ants apply abdominal gland secretions to their cuticle; formic acid detoxifies the venom; this probably contributes substantially to their ability to displace fire ants

items.notes: Area: natural science (invasion ecology). Key B. Band 7 moves: hedged dual purpose (identifies a behavior, suggests how it may help), key paraphrased away from the passage (no ant names, venom or formic acid in it), three wrong options open with a true first part (a chemical defense in an invasive ant; how an ant protects itself from a rival’s venom; a chemical the ant makes) and fail on a later link (stance, invented conclusion, function). Abstract wording kept in strength: ‘probably contributes substantially’ is the paper’s phrase.

fixes: coauthor’s first name corrected from Nicole to Nathan Jones (Crossref, Science 2014)
option C rewritten: it failed on its first part (‘native’ ruled out by ‘from South America’); now a true first part with an invented conclusion

band7.why: Hedged dual-purpose key of 24 words (identifies a behavior, suggests how it may help) paraphrased away from the passage, as in 82cb7dda; after the C rewrite all three distractors open with a true description and fail on one later link (stance, invented conclusion, function).

items.passage:
The following text is from Clarissa Scott Delany’s 1926 poem “The Mask.”

So detached and cool she is
No motion e’er betrays
The secret life within her soul,
The anguish of her days.

She seems to look upon the world
With cold ironic eyes,
To spurn emotion’s fevered sway,
To scoff at tears and sighs.

But once a woman with a child
Passed by her on the street,
And once she heard from casual lips
A man’s name, bitter-sweet.

Such baffled yearning in her eyes,
Such pain upon her face!
I turned aside until the mask
Was slipped once more in place.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that the woman’s outward coldness is a reaction to the speaker’s close observation of her
To reveal that the woman’s coldness is a pretense, one she gives up once she decides to confide in the speaker
To contrast the woman’s indifference toward strangers with her devotion to her own child and husband
To portray a woman whose composure hides a private sorrow that chance reminders briefly expose
items.explanation: The first two stanzas describe a woman who seems “detached and cool,” with “cold ironic eyes,” while “no motion” betrays “the anguish of her days.” The last two stanzas describe two chance moments, seeing a woman with a child and hearing a man’s name, that bring “baffled yearning” and “pain” to her face until her composure returns. The poem’s purpose is to portray a woman whose calm hides a private sorrow that such reminders briefly reveal, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The woman does appear cold, but the poem never links this to the speaker; the speaker only turns aside, out of tact, when her pain shows.

B.recipe: first part true, later link invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: Her coldness is indeed a pretense (the “mask”), but she never confides in the speaker: the speaker turns aside, and the mask is “slipped once more in place.”

C.why_wrong: She does seem indifferent, but the woman with a child is a stranger who passes by, and the man’s name is heard from “casual lips”; the poem mentions no child or husband of her own.

sources.what: text of “The Mask” as printed in Caroling Dusk (ed. Countee Cullen, 1927), Project Gutenberg #76889
“The Mask” first published in Palms, 1926

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1926, public domain in the US). Whole poem, copied exactly from Caroling Dusk (Gutenberg #76889); first publication Palms 1926. This is Clarissa Scott Delany (1901–1927), not the novelist Samuel R. Delany of the official Words in Context and Rhetorical Synthesis items. Hard band 6: two-part key (outward composure, hidden sorrow briefly exposed) kept free of the word ‘mask’; A, B and C open with a true observation (her coldness, her indifference) and fail later. Length 98 words with the attribution against models of 77 to 122; the poem is whole, so no lines were cut.

fixes: option B rewritten: the literal-disguise reading failed on its first part; now a true first part (the coldness is a pretense) with an invented later link (she confides in the speaker)

band7.why: P_lit band 6 by plan: two-part key (composure, sorrow briefly exposed) kept free of ‘mask’; A, B and C have true first parts. Length: 102 words, a whole 16-line poem, accepted: the turn needs both setup stanzas, and it sits inside the hard range (models 77, 79, 122).

items.passage: From 1943 to 1947, the Council on Books in Wartime, an organization of American publishers, distributed free paperbacks to US service members overseas. Printed inexpensively on digest-magazine presses and sized to fit in a uniform pocket, the books reached soldiers in hospitals, aboard troopships, and at remote outposts supplied by airdrop; <u>just before the 1944 invasion of Normandy, every soldier boarding a transport in southern England was handed one</u>. Historians of publishing credit the program with demonstrating that inexpensive paperbacks could attract an enormous readership, partly because it transformed so many young servicemen into habitual readers.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It gives a vivid instance of how thoroughly the books reached soldiers, which lends weight to the account of the program’s influence in the final sentence.
It offers a memorable example of the program’s reach, one that the text suggests persuaded military officials to keep distributing the books after the war ended.
It describes a moment when soldiers received the books, which the text presents as evidence that the titles were chosen mainly to prepare troops for combat.
It mentions a well-known military operation in order to show that the books were valued most by soldiers who were about to go into battle.
items.explanation: The second sentence lists the places the books reached, and the underlined portion caps the list with a striking case: every soldier boarding a transport before the Normandy invasion was handed a book. The final sentence says historians credit the program with proving that cheap paperbacks could find a vast audience, partly because it made readers of “so many young servicemen.” The underlined portion therefore illustrates the program’s reach, which supports that account of its influence, as choice A says.

B.recipe: first part true, later link invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The portion does show the program’s reach, and distribution did run to 1947, but the text never says this example, or anything else, persuaded officials to continue the program.

C.why_wrong: The portion does describe soldiers receiving books, but the text says nothing about how titles were chosen or about preparing troops for combat.

D.why_wrong: The portion does mention the Normandy invasion, but the text never ranks which soldiers valued the books most; it uses the handout to show how widely the books reached soldiers, which supports the final sentence.

sources.what: Armed Services Editions 1943–1947: small paperbacks that fit a uniform pocket, printed on digest-magazine presses, given free to soldiers; nearly 123 million copies; Mott: they ‘made book readers of hundreds of thousands of young men’; Hackenberg: the series ‘set the final imprimatur on cheap, mass-market reading material’

Wikipedia, Armed Services Editions (citing Cole 1984, p. 9): distribution 1943 to 1947 to hospitals, transports and air-dropped to remote outposts; before the Normandy invasion each man received a book as he embarked his invasion transport

items.notes: Area: history (publishing, World War II). Key A. Band 7 moves: the span is a single case whose job is to show extent (not a number, to avoid cloning 3.12’s ‘more than 7,000 in all’), and the key ties it to the claim in the following sentence (the deciding clue comes after the span). B, C, and D each open with a true description of the span and fail on a later link (persuaded officials, purpose of titles, an invented ranking of which soldiers valued the books most). Distribution to hospitals, transports, and remote outposts by airdrop and the pre-Normandy handout (each man received a book as he boarded his invasion transport) follow Cole 1984 as summarized on Wikipedia’s Armed Services Editions page; the influence claim is softened to ‘helping to prove that inexpensive paperbacks could find a vast audience’ (Wikipedia: ‘helped to prove the viability of paperback publishing’).

fixes: option D rewritten: the date alone (1943 vs 1944) ruled it out; now a true first part with an invented comparison
added the Wikipedia ASE source that carries the Normandy handout

band7.why: Span is a single case showing extent (like 2e744883’s ‘more than 7,000’), the deciding sentence follows the span, key 27 words with a compound clause; after the D rewrite every distractor has a true first part and an invented later link.

items.passage: In 1942, as Japanese Americans on the West Coast were being forcibly removed to incarceration camps, sculptor Isamu Noguchi, a New York resident exempt from the order, voluntarily entered the camp at Poston, Arizona, intending to make conditions there more humane. He drafted plans for the camp: <u>his blueprints designated space not only for an arts center, botanical gardens, and a cemetery but even for a zoo and a miniature golf course</u>. Within months, however, having received no support from camp administrators and feeling increasingly isolated, Noguchi was requesting his release; none of his designs was ever constructed.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It conveys how far-reaching Noguchi’s plans for the camp were, a scope that, according to the text, persuaded officials to grant his request to leave.
It lists facilities that Noguchi designed for the camp, which the text indicates were later built in simpler form by the people incarcerated there.
It conveys how ambitious Noguchi’s hopes for the camp were, which sharpens the contrast with the outcome described in the final sentence.
It describes plans that Noguchi made at Poston in order to show that his experience there shaped the sculptures he produced after the war.
items.explanation: The text says Noguchi entered Poston hoping to make life there more humane, and the underlined portion shows how far his plans went: beyond an arts center and gardens to a zoo and a miniature golf course. The final sentence then turns: officials gave no support, he soon sought release, and none of the designs was built. The underlined portion conveys the scale of his hopes, which heightens the contrast with that outcome, as choice C says.

A.recipe: first part true, causal link invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The portion does show how far-reaching the plans were, but the text says officials gave him no support and that he sought release; it never says the plans persuaded officials of anything.

B.why_wrong: The portion does list facilities Noguchi designed, but the final sentence says none of his designs was ever built, in any form.

D.why_wrong: The portion does describe Noguchi’s plans for Poston, but the text never mentions his later sculpture or any effect the camp had on it.

sources.what: Noguchi, a New York resident not subject to Executive Order 9066, entered Poston voluntarily in 1942; blueprints for an arts center, market, cemetery, gardens, a zoo, and a miniature golf course; no support from the War Relocation Authority or Poston officials; by August he pleaded for release, feeling isolated; none of the designs was realized

items.notes: Area: humanities and history (art, Japanese American incarceration). Key C. Band 7 moves: the span is a single case (two unexpected facilities) whose job is to show the extent of Noguchi’s hopes, and its function depends on the turn in the following sentence (‘however … none of his designs was ever built’); all three wrong options open with a true description of the span and fail on a later link (causal, outcome, purpose). Kept to the Poston episode, not Noguchi’s career, and the key avoids 3.10’s ‘helps explain … position’ frame.

band7.why: Span conveys ambition and its job depends on the ‘however’ turn after it; key needs the final sentence; all three distractors describe the span correctly and fail on a later link (B by reversal against the turn, as in band-7 officials).

items.passage: Dogs’ proficiency at following human pointing gestures has frequently been cited as evidence that domestication endowed dogs with a distinctive sensitivity to human communication, but that conclusion may be premature. In a 2008 study, Monique Udell, Nicole Dorey, and Clive Wynne tested wolves that had been hand-reared by people and socialized with them daily. Without any training, the wolves used a momentary pointing gesture by a distant experimenter to locate concealed food, whereas dogs living in a shelter, as well as pet dogs tested outdoors, generally failed to do so.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes research comparing wolves and dogs in order to establish that wolves are generally more skilled than dogs at interpreting human communication.
It presents the study by Udell, Dorey, and Wynne to explain how dogs gradually acquired their skill at following human gestures during domestication.
It describes a 2008 study in order to criticize the methods that earlier researchers had used to test dogs’ responses to human pointing.
It discusses a study of wolves raised by people to suggest that an ability often credited to domestication might not depend on it.
items.explanation: The text opens with a common claim, that dogs’ skill at following pointing shows domestication gave them a special sensitivity, and warns that this conclusion “may be premature.” It then describes a study in which wolves raised by people followed a pointing gesture to food without training, while shelter dogs and pet dogs tested outdoors generally did not. The study is presented to suggest that the ability may not depend on domestication, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text does compare wolves with some dogs, but it uses the result to caution about a claim concerning domestication; it does not try to show that wolves are generally better at reading people than dogs are.

B.why_wrong: The text does present this study, but the study suggests the ability need not come from domestication; it does not trace how dogs acquired it.

C.why_wrong: The text does describe a 2008 study, but it questions a conclusion drawn from dogs’ behavior, not the methods of earlier experiments, which it never describes.

sources.what: Udell, Dorey, Wynne (Animal Behaviour 2008), abstract: hand-reared, well-socialized wolves followed momentary distal human points to food without training; shelter dogs and dogs tested outdoors did not, pet dogs tested indoors did; domestication is not required for human-like social cognition in canids

items.notes: Area: social science and behavior (animal cognition). Key D. Band 7 moves: hedged dual purpose (discusses a study to suggest an ability might not depend on domestication), the cautionary first sentence must be folded into the key, every wrong option keeps the right study and changes the purpose (overreach, reversal, stance). The passage does not mention that pet dogs tested indoors did follow the points; it says shelter dogs and outdoor-tested pet dogs ‘generally failed’, matching the abstract. Replaces an earlier claim on the BBC brain-training study (too widely reported).

band7.why: View-then-caution with a hedged dual-purpose key as in c61a7c4a; every distractor keeps the study and changes the purpose (overreach, reversal, stance); the cautionary first sentence must be folded into the key.

items.passage: In the 1960s, folklorist Alan Lomax and collaborators at Columbia University launched Cantometrics, an ambitious project that sought to correlate the singing styles of the world’s cultures with their patterns of social organization. Rather than transcribing melodies, the team rated approximately 4,000 recorded songs from roughly 400 societies on 37 characteristics, including the degree of tension in singers’ voices and the extent to which members of a group blended together. Some musicologists, however, doubted that any quantity of such ratings could establish reliable connections between a community’s music and its social structure.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a project linking music to society, describes the procedure used to analyze songs, and then conveys some scholars’ doubts about what that procedure could show.
It presents a project that compared music across cultures, explains why its researchers preferred rating recordings to transcribing them, and then notes an objection to that preference.
It introduces a cross-cultural study of singing, details how the songs were assessed, and then describes how the study’s methods were revised in response to its critics.
It describes the goal of a large research project, outlines the procedure its team followed, and then reports a result that the team regarded as confirming that goal.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Cantometrics and its aim of relating singing styles to how cultures are organized. The second describes the team’s procedure: rating some 4,000 songs on 37 features. The third reports that some musicologists doubted such ratings could establish reliable links between music and social structure. Choice A follows these three moves in order.

B.recipe: move 1 right, move 2 overstated, move 3 wrong target (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text says the team rated songs “rather than transcribing melodies” but gives no reason for that choice, and the musicologists doubted what the ratings could prove, not the decision to rate instead of transcribe.

C.why_wrong: The project and its procedure are described, but the text ends with the critics’ doubts; it never says the methods were revised.

D.why_wrong: The text reports no result at all, and its final sentence casts doubt on the project’s aim rather than confirming it.

sources.what: Cantometrics: Lomax and a team at Columbia, proposed 1959, 37 style factors rated by observers, about 4,000 songs from over 400 cultures, aim to relate song style to social organization; some critics questioned whether one could ever have enough statistics to prove anything about music and culture

items.notes: Area: humanities (music, ethnomusicology). Key A. Hard band 6 (S14 has no band-7 official). Three-move key in abstract nouns; B, C and D keep move 1 (and C and D move 2) and fail on a later move, as 3.9’s hard distractors do. The critique sentence paraphrases the source without strengthening it (‘doubted that any quantity of such ratings could establish reliable links’ for ‘questioned whether one could ever have enough statistics to prove anything about music and culture’).

band7.why: S14 has no band-7 official item, so a strong band 6: three-move abstract key; B, C and D keep move 1 (C and D move 2) and fail later.

items.passage: Copepods of the genus Calanus, minute crustaceans abundant in northern seas, ascend toward the surface at dusk and descend into deeper water at dawn, a schedule that allows them to graze on surface phytoplankton under cover of darkness while remaining invisible during daylight to fish, which are visual predators. Numerous other zooplankton follow the same daily schedule. In Dabob Bay, Washington, however, Mark Ohman and colleagues discovered that the copepod Pseudocalanus does the reverse, ascending by day and descending at night, apparently to avoid invertebrate predators that themselves migrate upward after dark.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It accounts for a daily pattern of movement in one group of animals, observes that the pattern is common, and then describes a population whose contrary habit has yet to be explained.
It describes a daily movement and the reason for it, indicates that many organisms share it, and then reports evidence that the movement is less widespread than once assumed.
It explains why one kind of animal moves as it does each day, notes that this movement is widespread, and then presents a population that moves the opposite way for a comparable reason.
It identifies a daily pattern and its cause, states that the pattern is typical of similar organisms, and then explains how one population changed its pattern after a new predator appeared.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes Calanus copepods’ daily rise and fall and explains it (feeding at night while avoiding fish that hunt by sight). The second says many other zooplankton do the same. The third presents Pseudocalanus in Dabob Bay, which does the reverse, apparently to avoid predators that rise at night, so it too is avoiding predators. Choice C follows these moves, including the fact that the exception has a comparable explanation.

A.why_wrong: The text does give an explanation for the opposite habit: Pseudocalanus apparently avoids invertebrate predators that rise after dark.

B.why_wrong: The text presents one population that does the opposite; it never suggests that the usual movement is less common than researchers thought.

D.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 invented change over time (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text describes Pseudocalanus’s reverse migration and its likely reason, but says nothing about a change in its behavior or the arrival of a new predator.

sources.what: Ohman, Frost, Cohen (Science 1983): the copepod Pseudocalanus sp. shows reverse diel vertical migration in Dabob Bay, Washington, concurrently with normal vertical migration by nocturnal invertebrate predators; reduced overlap with predators appears to lower adult female mortality

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine ecology). Key C. band_target 6, not the plan’s 7: S16 has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md, section 1), so per WAVE.md it is written as a strong band 6. Three-move key; every wrong option keeps moves 1 and 2 (worded differently in each, to avoid a shared prefix) and breaks move 3 (unexplained, less widespread, changed after a new predator). The pattern move is one short sentence and the passage avoids 3.17’s cost and benefit wording; it centers on Pseudocalanus, unlike the served lanternfish and Arctic zooplankton items. The Calanus sentence gives the standard predator-avoidance account of normal vertical migration; the core claim checked is Ohman’s.

band7.why: S16 has no band-7 official item (the band-6 model 4ed09415 is the ceiling), so a strong band 6: all distractors keep moves 1 and 2 and break move 3.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Mór Jókai’s 1865 novel Debts of Honor (translated by Arthur B. Yolland in 1900). The narrator, a boy of ten, is being sent to live with a family in Pressburg in exchange for their daughter.

The journey to Pressburg lasted from early morning till late evening; only as twilight came on did a new thought begin to keep me awake: “What kind of a child could it be, for whom I was now being exchanged? Who was to usurp my place at table, in my bed-room, and in my mother’s heart? was she as much afraid of me as I was of her?”

For I was very much afraid of her.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the sights that the narrator notices during a long journey to a new town
To convey the narrator’s growing fear of the girl who will replace him at home
To explain why the narrator’s parents decided to send him away to Pressburg
To show the narrator’s eagerness to meet a girl who will become like a sister to him
items.explanation: As twilight falls on the journey, the narrator begins to wonder about the child “for whom I was now being exchanged”: who will “usurp my place at table, in my bed-room, and in my mother’s heart,” what she will be like, and whether she fears him as he fears her. He ends, “I was very much afraid of her.” The text conveys his growing fear of the girl who will replace him at home, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The journey is only the setting; the narrator describes no sights, only the questions that keep him awake.

C.why_wrong: The text never says why the exchange is being made; it focuses on the narrator’s thoughts about the girl.

D.why_wrong: The narrator is not eager: he worries that the girl will “usurp” his place and says he is “very much afraid of her.”

sources.what: text of Debts of Honor, chapter 1 (Yolland translation, Doubleday 1900), Project Gutenberg #22757
Hungarian original Mire megvénülünk, 1865; Yolland translation New York 1900
Hungarian Wikipedia: Mire megvénülünk, Jókai Mór írta, 1865-ben megjelent regény (second source for the year)

items.notes: Area: literature (Hungarian novel in a 1900 translation, public domain). Copied from Project Gutenberg #22757; ‘adapted’ because the opening sentence of the paragraph (‘Of the impressions of the journey … in the carriage.’) and four questions (‘Was she small or large? beautiful or ugly? obedient or contrary? had she brothers or sisters, to whom I was to be a brother?’) are left out, as is the clause ‘a thought to which as yet I had paid no attention’ (cut in review for length), and the source’s double hyphen is not used. The context line follows the chapter (‘The Girl Substitute’; the girl is to take ‘my place as my mother’s child, giving me instead her own parents’). Key B. Year 1865 for Mire megvénülünk from Hungarian bibliographic records.

fixes: cut the clause ‘a thought to which as yet I had paid no attention’ (128 to 117 words, models’ median 96)
added a second source for the 1865 date (Hungarian Wikipedia)

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Emilia Pardo Bazán’s 1885 novel The Swan of Vilamorta (translated by Mary J. Serrano in 1891). Segundo García is a young man from Vilamorta, a town in Galicia, Spain.

Segundo composed his first verses, cynical and pessimistic in intention, ingenuous in reality, before he had reached the age of seventeen. His classmates applauded him to the echo. He acquired in their eyes a certain prestige. Thenceforth he acquired the right to indulge in solitary walks, to laugh rarely, to surround his adventures with mystery, and not to play or take a drink for good-fellowship’s sake except when he felt in the humor.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray how early praise from his classmates led a young poet to cultivate an air of mystery
To explain why Segundo’s classmates came to resent the attention and prestige that his first poems brought him
To show that Segundo’s first poems were admired by readers and critics throughout Spain
To suggest that Segundo later came to regret the gloomy and cynical tone of the poems he wrote as a youth
items.explanation: The text says Segundo wrote his first verses before seventeen, that his classmates “applauded him to the echo,” and that he gained “a certain prestige” in their eyes. With that prestige he “acquired the right” to take solitary walks, laugh rarely, and surround himself with mystery. The text thus portrays how early praise from his classmates led him to cultivate an aloof, mysterious manner, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: His classmates applauded him and gave him prestige; nothing suggests resentment.

C.why_wrong: The admiration described comes from his classmates; the text gives no sign of readers throughout Spain.

D.why_wrong: The text calls the verses “pessimistic in intention,” but it never says Segundo regretted their tone; it shows him building on their success.

sources.what: text of The Swan of Vilamorta, translated by Mary J. Serrano (Cassell, 1891), Project Gutenberg #54105

items.notes: Area: literature (Spanish novel El cisne de Vilamorta, 1885, in an 1891 translation, public domain). Copied from Project Gutenberg #54105; ‘adapted’ because the third sentence ends at ‘prestige’ (the source continues ‘and when the first fruits of his muse appeared in a periodical he had, without going beyond the narrow circle of the college, admirers and detractors’). The context line uses the hero’s full name as the novel gives it. Key A. The narrator’s irony (‘acquired the right to’) is the point of the purpose key.

items.passage: Packrats, rodents inhabiting the deserts of western North America, construct their dens from twigs, leaves, seeds, and other material collected within a short distance of home. Such accumulations, called middens, would ordinarily decompose or disperse, but <u>the rats urinate on them, and in arid air the urine crystallizes into a hard, amber-like substance called amberat that cements the debris together and dramatically slows its decay</u>. Because some middens have persisted as long as 40,000 years, researchers such as Julio Betancourt have reconstructed how desert vegetation has changed by dating and identifying the plant fragments preserved inside them.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes how packrats decide which plants to collect for their middens.
It explains why packrats prefer to build their middens in especially dry places.
It describes a technique that researchers use to date the remains found in middens.
It explains how the plant material in packrat middens comes to be preserved.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined portion says middens would ordinarily decay. The underlined portion explains why they do not: the rats’ urine crystallizes into amberat, which cements the debris and slows its decay. The last sentence then explains why that matters to researchers. The portion describes how the plant material in middens is preserved, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says only that packrats gather material near their dens; the underlined portion is about what happens to the pile afterward, not how plants are chosen.

B.why_wrong: The portion mentions dry air as a condition for the urine to crystallize, but it says nothing about where packrats prefer to build.

C.why_wrong: Dating the remains is mentioned in the last sentence as something researchers do; the underlined portion describes a natural process caused by the rats.

sources.what: packrat middens: urine crystallizes into amberat, an asphalt-like crust that can preserve plant material for tens of thousands of years; Betancourt’s work (Packrat Middens: The Last 40,000 Years of Biotic Change, 1990)

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleoecology). Key D. Medium F_method on the model of 2.15 (a mechanism stated in the underlined portion, set between a problem and a research payoff). Material gathered within a short distance of the den and the slowing of decay follow Betancourt, Van Devender and Martin (1990) as summarized on Wikipedia’s Pack rat page; Julio Betancourt is a USGS scientist who co-edited that book.

items.passage: Culture, in the sense of behavior transmitted between individuals through social learning rather than through genes, has been documented most extensively in primates, but whales may rival them. <u>Since about 1980, a feeding technique in which a humpback whale strikes the water with its tail before releasing a net of bubbles around a school of fish has spread through the humpback population of the Gulf of Maine.</u> Analyzing 27 years of observations, Jenny Allen and her colleagues determined that whales were considerably more likely to adopt the technique if they had associated with whales already using it.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes a feeding behavior that the following sentence shows to be inherited from parents rather than learned from other whales.
It explains how the technique lets humpbacks catch more fish than bubble nets alone would.
It introduces a case that the text goes on to use as evidence for the first sentence’s suggestion.
It describes a technique that researchers taught to captive whales to measure how quickly whales learn.
items.explanation: The first sentence suggests that whales may rival primates in having culture, behavior spread by social learning. The underlined sentence introduces a specific case, a feeding technique that spread through the Gulf of Maine humpbacks. The last sentence shows that the technique spread through social contact, which supports the first sentence. The underlined sentence thus presents a case that the text uses as evidence, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The following sentence shows the opposite: whales adopted the technique after associating with whales that used it, which is social learning, not inheritance.

B.why_wrong: The sentence describes what the technique involves and how it spread; it never compares how many fish whales catch with and without the tail slap.

D.why_wrong: The technique arose among wild whales and was observed over 27 years; no one taught it to captive whales.

sources.what: Allen, Weinrich, Hoppitt, Rendell (Science 2013): network-based diffusion analysis shows the cultural spread of lobtail feeding through a humpback whale population over 27 years; models with social transmission strongly supported

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key C. Medium F_example in the manner of 2.12 (a general claim, then an underlined specific case, then the study) without its ‘Consider …’ opener. Lobtail feeding (one to four tail slaps on the surface before a bubble-feeding sequence) was first recorded in one Gulf of Maine whale in 1980 (University of St Andrews news release, 2013); the passage says ‘since about 1980’. Distractor B avoids prey choice, since the behavior’s rise is linked in the paper to sand lance, a fact the passage leaves out. Replaces an earlier claim on the chewed birch pitch genome (too widely reported).

items.passage: In 1969 a group of Chicano artists in Sacramento, California, among them José Montoya and Esteban Villa, formed a collective to support the farmworkers’ labor movement and to bring art to Mexican American neighborhoods. They called themselves the Rebel Chicano Art Front, but because people repeatedly mistook the initials RCAF for those of the Royal Canadian Air Force, the artists good-humoredly renamed the group the Royal Chicano Air Force. Its members subsequently produced murals and silkscreen posters, many decorated with old-fashioned biplanes, and in 1972 they established a community arts center in Sacramento.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why a group of artists chose to model its posters on the ones once used to recruit military pilots
To trace how an artists’ collective formed, how it got its name, and what it went on to create
To argue that a collective’s sense of humor weakened the political message of its art
To compare the posters made by one collective with murals made by other artists in California
items.explanation: The text says when, where, and why the collective formed, explains how a confusion over its initials led the artists to rename it the Royal Chicano Air Force, and then describes its later work: murals, posters, and a community arts center. Choice B covers all three parts: the group’s origins, its name, and its work.

A.why_wrong: The posters are said to be decorated with biplanes, a joke on the group’s name; the text never mentions recruiting posters or explains the posters’ design.

C.why_wrong: The text presents the group’s humor neutrally and makes no judgment about its political message.

D.why_wrong: No other artists are mentioned, and the text compares nothing.

sources.what: Royal Chicano Air Force archives finding aid (UC Santa Barbara): started in 1969 to support the Chicano movement and the United Farm Workers; first called the Rebel Chicano Art Front, renamed in good humor after the initials were mistaken for the Royal Canadian Air Force; founders include José Montoya and Esteban Villa; silkscreen posters using World War I aviators and biplanes; murals; Centro de Artistas Chicanos founded 1972

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (Chicano art). Key B. Medium P_profile on the model of 2.5 (origins, then development). The founding year follows the UCSB finding aid (1969); some sources give 1970. ‘Bring art to Mexican American neighborhoods’ paraphrases the group’s aim of public arts and cultural programs; the 1972 center is the Centro de Artistas Chicanos.

items.passage: <u>A city’s linguistic landscape is the collection of languages visible on its public signage, from street names to commercial storefronts.</u> Studying it can reveal which languages a community chooses to display and who makes those choices. In a survey published in 2007, linguist Peter Backhaus examined roughly 12,000 signs near 28 train stations in central Tokyo and found that about one in five was multilingual. Most of those multilingual signs had been put up not by government agencies but by shops and other private businesses.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It defines a concept that the text then applies to one city.
It summarizes a finding that the rest of the text calls into question.
It describes a method that the researcher in the text later revised.
It identifies a problem that the researcher in the text set out to solve.
items.explanation: The first sentence explains what a city’s linguistic landscape is: the languages visible on its public signs. The next sentence says why it is worth studying, and the rest of the text describes Backhaus’s survey of the linguistic landscape of central Tokyo. The first sentence therefore defines a concept that the text then applies to a particular city, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The first sentence reports no finding, and nothing later in the text questions it.

C.why_wrong: The first sentence defines a term rather than describing a method, and the text never says Backhaus revised anything.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the first sentence is presented as a problem; Backhaus surveyed signs to describe them, not to solve anything.

sources.what: review of Backhaus, Linguistic Landscapes: A Comparative Study of Urban Multilingualism in Tokyo (Multilingual Matters, 2007): about 12,000 signs sampled near the entrances of 28 stations on the Yamanote Line, 2,444 multilingual; multilingual signs mostly non-official; definition of linguistic landscape after Landry and Bourhis (1997)

items.notes: Area: social science (sociolinguistics). Key A. Medium F_term on the model of 2.3 (the first sentence defines the term; options are four relation labels), with the stem ‘function of the first sentence’ and the sentence also underlined, as in the official item. 2,444 of about 12,000 is ‘about one in five’.

items.passage:
The following text is from Sergei Aksakov’s 1856 memoir A Russian Gentleman (translated by J. D. Duff in 1917). Sofya Nikolayevna and her husband, Alexyei Stepanitch, have recently married and are living in the town of Ufa.

Sofya Nikolayevna arranged her engagements in the town in accordance with her own wishes. The people whom she liked she often met, either in their houses or her own; the rest she seldom saw, and was content to exchange formal calls with them. Her husband was acquainted already with everybody in the town; but his wife’s intimate friends now became intimate with him. He became popular with them and got on very well in his new position<u>—I mean, in the select society that gathered round his wife</u>.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals that Alexyei Stepanitch resents the influence his wife has over their social life.
It emphasizes that Alexyei Stepanitch had already met everyone in the town before his marriage.
It explains why Sofya Nikolayevna seldom visited the people she did not like.
It narrows an earlier claim about how well Alexyei Stepanitch got on in his new position.
items.explanation: Just before the underlined portion, the narrator says Alexyei “became popular” and “got on very well in his new position.” The underlined portion then limits that claim: his success was “in the select society that gathered round his wife,” not in the town as a whole. The portion narrows the earlier claim, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests resentment; Alexyei becomes friendly with his wife’s friends and gets on well among them.

B.why_wrong: An earlier sentence says he already knew everybody in the town; the underlined portion does something different, limiting where his popularity lay.

C.why_wrong: Sofya Nikolayevna’s habits are described in the earlier sentences; the underlined portion is about her husband and gives no reason for her choices.

sources.what: text of A Russian Gentleman, translated by J. D. Duff (Edward Arnold, 1917), Project Gutenberg #38781; the translator’s preface dates the complete work to 1856 and calls Aksakov’s books memoirs

items.notes: Area: literature (Russian family chronicle, 1856, in a 1917 translation, public domain). One paragraph copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #38781; the source’s double hyphen printed as a closed em dash. Genre ‘memoir’ follows Duff, who calls Aksakov’s books his memoirs. Key D. Medium F_qualify on the model of 2.4 (a short span that limits an earlier description, ‘a soft kind of rock’); the key avoids that item’s wording ‘qualifies an earlier description’. Passage 121 words with the attribution (2.4: 114).

items.passage:
The following text is from Effie Lee Newsome’s poem “Sky Pictures,” published in the 1927 anthology Caroling Dusk. The speaker has been watching clouds shaped like polar bears, mountains, and sheep.

The polar bears would like to get
Where polar bears belong.
The mountains try so hard to stand
In one place firm and strong.
The little sheep all want to stop
And pasture in the sky,
But never can these things be done,
Although they try and try!
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker describes clouds breaking apart and then explains what causes them to form again.
The speaker praises the strength of the shapes in the clouds and then predicts that the shapes will last.
The speaker describes what the cloud shapes are striving for and then admits that they cannot succeed.
The speaker imagines animals living in the sky and then wishes that she could join them there.
items.explanation: The first six lines describe what each cloud shape seems to want: the polar bears to reach where they belong, the mountains to stand firm in one place, the sheep to stop and graze. The last two lines say “never can these things be done, / Although they try and try!” The speaker describes the shapes’ efforts and then acknowledges a limit, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The lines say nothing about how clouds form or break apart; they describe what the shapes seem to want.

B.recipe: first move partly right, second reversed (REV)
B.why_wrong: The mountains do try to stand “firm and strong,” but the speaker ends by saying the shapes can never do what they try to do, not that they will last.

D.why_wrong: The speaker imagines the shapes’ wishes, not her own, and never wishes to join them.

sources.what: text of “Sky Pictures” by Mary Effie Lee Newsome in Caroling Dusk (ed. Countee Cullen, Harper, 1927), Project Gutenberg #76889

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, public domain in the US). The last eight lines of the twenty-line poem, copied exactly from Caroling Dusk (Gutenberg #76889); the context line supplies what the first twelve lines establish (the shapes are clouds). The source line says where the poem was published rather than giving a first-publication year, which could not be confirmed (Newsome placed poems in The Crisis and The Brownies’ Book in the early 1920s). Key C. Medium S4 on the model of 2.8 (efforts, then a limit). Replaces an earlier claim on Henry Kendall’s ‘The Voice in the Wild Oak’, whose shortest two-move excerpt ran about 140 words against the model’s 63.

items.passage: It is often assumed that few people in early medieval England lived much past the age of 45, an impression reinforced by cemetery studies, which typically place every adult over 45 in a single age category because skeletal methods of estimating age become unreliable after that point. In 2016, however, archaeologists Christine Cave and Marc Oxenham reexamined adults buried in Worthy Park, an Anglo-Saxon cemetery, by ranking them according to the wear on their teeth. Their analysis suggested that many of those individuals had died well after 45, some in their seventies.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a method that archaeologists use to estimate ages, then explains why that method suits early medieval remains.
It presents a common belief about life spans in an earlier era and what reinforced it, then describes research that challenges that belief.
It describes a debate between two archaeologists, then presents evidence that settles the debate in favor of one of them.
It identifies a gap in the burial records of an Anglo-Saxon cemetery, then explains how researchers filled that gap by excavating a set of new graves.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents a common assumption (few early medieval people lived much past 45) and the cemetery practice that reinforces it. The second and third sentences describe Cave and Oxenham’s tooth-wear study, which suggested that many adults at Worthy Park died well after 45. Choice B describes this structure: a common belief and its support, then research that challenges it.

A.why_wrong: The text says skeletal methods become unreliable after 45; it never argues that a method suits early medieval remains, and its main point is the challenge to a common belief.

C.why_wrong: Cave and Oxenham worked together; the text describes no disagreement between them.

D.recipe: first move partly right, second invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text concerns how ages are estimated, not missing records, and the researchers reexamined burials already excavated rather than digging new graves.

sources.what: Cave and Oxenham, ‘Identification of the Archaeological “Invisible Elderly”: An Approach Illustrated with an Anglo-Saxon Example’ (International Journal of Osteoarchaeology 26, 2016): occlusal tooth wear used to order adults at Worthy Park; about two-thirds of adults previously placed in a single 45+ category redistributed into age groups from the mid-40s to the mid-70s

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology). Key B. Medium S8 on the model of 2.17 (common view, then a recent finding that challenges it). The passage claims no more than the source: ‘many … had died well after 45, some in their seventies’ for about two-thirds of the 45+ adults redistributed into groups from the mid-40s to the mid-70s. Cave and Oxenham ordered the sample by wear and assigned ages using a Hadza mortality profile; ‘ranking them according to the wear on their teeth’ simplifies that.

items.passage:
The following text is from Hjalmar Hjorth Boyesen’s 1892 story collection Boyhood in Norway. Marcus, a storekeeper’s son, greatly admires Viggo, the son of an army colonel. Marcus has been hit by a thrown stone while bringing Viggo a message.

A doctor was now sent for; the stone was cut out without difficulty, and Marcus was invited to remain as Viggo’s guest until he recovered. <u>He felt so honored by this invitation that he secretly prayed he might remain ill for a month</u>; but the wound showed an abominable readiness to heal, and before three days were past Marcus could not feign any ailment which his face and eye did not belie.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It shows how much Marcus values the chance to stay with Viggo.
It suggests that Marcus is worried that his wound will not heal.
It reveals that Viggo’s family is eager for Marcus to leave their home.
It explains why the doctor was able to remove the stone so easily.
items.explanation: Marcus admires Viggo, and the text says he is invited to stay as Viggo’s guest until he recovers. The underlined portion says he was so honored that he secretly hoped to stay ill for a month, which shows how much the invitation means to him, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: Marcus hopes to stay ill longer; he is not worried that the wound will fail to heal, and the text says it healed quickly.

C.why_wrong: Viggo’s family invited Marcus to stay; nothing suggests they want him gone.

D.why_wrong: The ease of the operation is mentioned earlier in the sentence before; the underlined portion is about Marcus’s feelings, not the doctor.

sources.what: text of “The Battle of the Rafts” in Boyhood in Norway (1892), Project Gutenberg #784

items.notes: Area: literature (story collection, 1892, public domain). Copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #784, ‘The Battle of the Rafts’; the context lines follow the story (Viggo Hook is the eldest son of Colonel Hook; Marcus’s father keeps a store; Marcus was hit by a sling stone while carrying a warning to Viggo). Key A. Easy F_lit on the model of 1.20 (a detail that shows a feeling).

items.passage:
The following text is from Eleanor H. Porter’s 1916 novel Just David. David, a boy who carries his violin everywhere, has wandered onto the grounds of a wealthy woman’s country home.

The Wonder, in Hinsdale parlance, was only Miss Holbrook’s garden, but in David’s eyes it was fairyland come true. For one whole minute <u>he could only stand like a very ordinary little boy and stare</u>. At the end of the minute he became himself once more; and being himself, he expressed his delight at once in the only way he knew how to do—by raising his violin and beginning to play.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that David is unsure whether he is allowed to be in the garden.
It indicates that David is too tired from his long walk to play his violin.
It reveals that David has seen many gardens like this one before.
It conveys how amazed David is by the garden he has found.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one says the garden was “fairyland come true” in David’s eyes. The underlined portion says that for a whole minute he could only stand and stare, which shows how amazed he is, before he expresses his delight by playing. Choice D states this function.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests David worries about being allowed in the garden; he stares in wonder and then plays.

B.why_wrong: David is not too tired to play: after the minute passes, he raises his violin and begins playing at once.

C.why_wrong: The garden seems “fairyland come true” to David, which suggests he has never seen anything like it.

sources.what: text of Just David (1916), Project Gutenberg #440

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1916, public domain). One paragraph copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #440 (chapter ‘The Lady of the Roses’); the source’s double hyphen printed as a closed em dash. Context line: David has followed a path into Sunny-crest, the country home of Miss Barbara Holbrook, Hinsdale’s one rich resident. Key D.

items.passage: Victoria Santa Cruz, born in Lima, Peru, in 1922 into a family of Black artists and musicians, became a central figure in Afro-Peruvian culture. In 1958 she and her brother Nicomedes founded Cumanana, Peru’s first Black theater company. After studying theater and choreography in Paris, she established the troupe Teatro y Danzas Negras del Perú in 1966. The company revived traditional Afro-Peruvian dances and presented them to audiences internationally. In 1978 she composed and performed the poem “Me gritaron negra” (“They Shouted ‘Black’ at Me”), an affirmation of pride in her Black identity.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Santa Cruz decided to study theater in Paris
To argue that Afro-Peruvian dance is better known abroad than in Peru
To give an overview of Santa Cruz’s work celebrating Afro-Peruvian culture
To compare Santa Cruz’s poetry with the plays written by her brother
items.explanation: The text traces Santa Cruz’s career: founding Peru’s first Black theater company with her brother, forming a troupe that revived Afro-Peruvian dances, and writing and performing a poem about pride in her Black identity. Its purpose is to give an overview of her work celebrating Afro-Peruvian culture, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that she studied in Paris but never says why, and that detail is only one step in her career.

B.why_wrong: The text says her troupe performed in Peru and abroad; it makes no argument about where the dances are better known.

D.why_wrong: Her brother is mentioned only as a cofounder of Cumanana; the text compares no works.

sources.what: Victoria Santa Cruz (1922–2014): born in Lima to a family of Black artists; cofounded Cumanana, Peru’s first Black theater company, with her brother Nicomedes in 1958; studied theater and choreography in Paris 1961–1965; founded Teatro y Danzas Negras del Perú in 1966; re-created dances such as landó; wrote and performed “Me Gritaron Negra” in 1978 about reclaiming her Black identity

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (dance, theater, Afro-Peruvian culture). Key C. Easy P_profile on the model of 1.6 and 1.10 (an overview of a figure’s work and significance). The poem’s title is given with an English gloss in parentheses; the translation is ours and kept literal.

items.passage:
The following text is from James Stephens’s 1912 novel Mary, Mary. Mary Makebelieve lives with her mother in Dublin, Ireland. She often walks in a park in the city.

Mary Makebelieve thought it was very clever of the little ducklings to be able to swim so well. She loved them, and when nobody was looking she used to cluck at them like their mother, but she did not often do this because she did not know duck language really well, and feared that her cluck might mean the wrong things, and that she might be giving these innocents bad advice, and telling them to do something contrary to what their mother had just directed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Mary learned to imitate the sounds that ducks make
To portray Mary’s affectionate and playful attitude toward the ducklings
To describe the advice that a mother duck gives to her young
To show that Mary is frightened of the ducks that live in the park
items.explanation: Mary thinks the ducklings are “very clever,” she “loved them,” and she clucks at them when no one is looking, while worrying, half in fun, that her cluck might give them bad advice. The text portrays her affectionate, playful attitude toward the ducklings, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says Mary does not know duck language well; it never describes how she learned to cluck.

C.why_wrong: The mother’s directions are mentioned only as something Mary fears she might contradict; the text never says what that advice is.

D.why_wrong: What Mary fears is giving the ducklings bad advice, not the ducks themselves; she loves them.

sources.what: text of Mary, Mary (Small, Maynard, 1912; published in Britain as The Charwoman’s Daughter), Project Gutenberg #24742

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1912, public domain). Copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #24742, the last two sentences of a paragraph about the ducklings in the park (the paragraph’s earlier sentences are not included, so ‘from’, not ‘adapted from’). Mary Makebelieve lives with her mother in Dublin; the park, with its lake, bridge and flower beds, is near Grafton Street. Key B.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Kate Chopin’s 1894 short story “A No-Account Creole.” Placide is engaged to Euphrasie, who is visiting New Orleans.

Placide was not very well acquainted with the city; but that made no difference to him so long as he was at Euphrasie’s side. He asked nothing better than to walk with Euphrasie along the streets, holding her parasol at an agreeable angle over her pretty head, or to sit beside her in the evening at the play, sharing her frank delight.

When the night of the Mardi Gras ball came, he felt like a lost spirit during the hours he was forced to remain away from her.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Placide refuses to learn his way around New Orleans
To describe the entertainments that New Orleans offers its visitors during Mardi Gras
To suggest that Euphrasie has grown tired of spending her time with Placide
To portray how happy Placide is simply to be in Euphrasie’s company
items.explanation: The text says it made no difference to Placide that he did not know the city as long as he was with Euphrasie, that he “asked nothing better” than to walk or sit beside her, and that he felt “like a lost spirit” when apart from her. The text portrays how happy he is just to be with her, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says only that Placide did not know the city well and did not mind; it never says he refuses to learn it.

B.why_wrong: The walks, the play, and the ball are mentioned only as occasions for Placide’s feelings; the text does not describe the city’s entertainments.

C.why_wrong: The text describes Placide’s feelings; the only hint of Euphrasie’s is her “frank delight” at the play, which he shares.

sources.what: text of “A No-Account Creole” in Bayou Folk (Houghton, Mifflin, 1894), Project Gutenberg #46650

items.notes: Area: literature (short story, 1894, public domain). Copied from Project Gutenberg #46650; ‘adapted’ because one sentence about Placide’s brother Hector is left out between the first and second sentences. Placide Santien is engaged to Euphrasie, who is in New Orleans for the Carnival season. Key D.

items.passage: Carnivorous plants, which capture animals to obtain nutrients that are scarce in their native soils, have evolved independently in several unrelated plant lineages. Most species capture insects with aboveground traps, such as adhesive leaves or fluid-filled pitchers. One unusual example is <u>Philcoxia, a diminutive plant of the sandy, nutrient-poor soils of central Brazil, whose tiny adhesive leaves lie just beneath the surface of the sand</u>. In 2012, Caio Pereira and his colleagues demonstrated that these subterranean leaves trap and digest microscopic worms called nematodes.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies a plant that serves as an unusual example of the carnivorous plants described earlier.
It explains why carnivorous plants usually grow in soils that lack nutrients.
It describes a method that researchers used to locate rare plants in Brazil.
It challenges the claim that carnivorous plants evolved in several groups.
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe carnivorous plants in general and say that most catch insects above ground. The underlined portion identifies Philcoxia, “one unusual example,” a plant whose sticky leaves lie underground, and the last sentence confirms that those leaves trap worms. Choice A states this function.

B.why_wrong: The first sentence mentions nutrient-poor soils; the underlined portion describes one particular plant and gives no reason for where carnivorous plants grow.

C.why_wrong: The portion describes the plant and where it grows; it says nothing about how researchers found it.

D.why_wrong: Philcoxia is presented as one more carnivorous plant, an unusual example, not as evidence against the first sentence.

sources.what: Pereira et al. (PNAS 2012), ‘Underground leaves of Philcoxia trap and digest nematodes’: Philcoxia of the Brazilian Cerrado, well-lit low-nutrient soils; subterranean adhesive leaves trap and digest nematodes

items.notes: Area: natural science (botany). Key A. Easy F_example on the model of 1.3 (a broad statement, then a specific example); the opener here is ‘One unusual example is’, not the official ‘One such’, and the underline covers the plant’s description rather than the whole sentence. Philcoxia grows in the Cerrado of central Brazil, in white sand, with leaves at or just below the surface.

items.passage: In 1982, residents of Apo Island in the Philippines, collaborating with marine scientists from nearby Silliman University, designated about 10 percent of their fishing reef as a reserve where all fishing was prohibited. The islanders enforced the prohibition themselves. Over the next 18 years, surveys by Garry Russ, Angel Alcala, and their colleagues documented a tripling of the biomass of surgeonfish and jacks, two important food fish, inside the reserve. The island’s catch of those fish was also higher in later years than before the reserve existed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that fishing should be banned on every reef near Apo Island
To compare the fish found near Apo Island with those found elsewhere in the Philippines
To describe how a community protected part of a reef and what happened as a result
To explain why surgeonfish and jacks are the most common fish near Apo Island
items.explanation: The text describes an effort, Apo Island residents banning fishing on part of their reef and enforcing the ban, and then reports its results: fish biomass in the reserve tripled and the islanders’ catch of those fish rose. Choice C covers both the effort and its results.

A.why_wrong: The text reports what happened after one reserve was created; it makes no argument for banning fishing on every reef.

B.why_wrong: No other places in the Philippines are mentioned.

D.why_wrong: Surgeonfish and jacks are mentioned only as fish whose numbers rose; the text does not say they are the most common or explain why.

sources.what: Russ, Alcala, Maypa, Calumpong, White (Ecological Applications 2004), ‘Marine reserve benefits local fisheries’: Apo Island no-take reserve (about 10 percent of the reef fishing area, protected from 1982); biomass of surgeonfish and jacks, 40 to 75 percent of the yield, tripled inside the reserve over 18 years; total catch higher after the reserve than before

items.notes: Area: natural and social science (marine conservation, community management). Key C. Easy P_effort on the model of 1.8 (an effort, then measured results); the key avoids 1.8’s wording ‘an effort made by … and some results of that effort’. Community enforcement and the Silliman University link follow the general accounts of the Apo reserve; the core claims checked are the paper’s. Replaces an earlier claim on Finland’s Housing First policy (a headline subject).

fixes: ‘The island’s total catch’ narrowed to ‘catch of those fish’: the source reports total catch of surgeonfish and jacks, not all fish; explanation matched

items.passage: In deserts, rainfall is infrequent, and seeds landing on parched ground rarely germinate. Some desert plants have evolved a solution: their seed capsules remain tightly closed in dry conditions and open only when moistened, releasing seeds when water is available. <u>Scientists call this behavior “hygrochasy.”</u> In 2011, Matthew Harrington and his colleagues investigated hygrochasy in an ice plant, Delosperma nakurense. They discovered that the capsule lids unfold when a layer of honeycomb-shaped cells absorbs rainwater. As the cells dry, the lids close again.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents a hypothesis that Harrington and his colleagues set out to test.
It gives the name for a plant behavior that the rest of the text discusses.
It summarizes the main result of the study described in the next sentence.
It explains why seeds rarely sprout when they land on dry ground.
items.explanation: The sentences before the underlined one describe a behavior: seed capsules that open only when wet. The underlined sentence gives that behavior a name, “hygrochasy,” and the rest of the text describes a study of it. Choice B states this function.

A.why_wrong: The sentence names a behavior; it does not propose anything to be tested.

items.passage: Did people in prehistoric Britain ever preserve their dead? <u>Archaeologist Mike Parker Pearson and his colleagues argue that at least some did.</u> At Cladh Hallan, a settlement on the Scottish island of South Uist, they excavated two skeletons buried about 3,000 years ago. Laboratory analyses indicated that the bodies had been deliberately placed in a nearby peat bog, where acidic, oxygen-poor conditions inhibited decomposition, and later retrieved. The individuals, it turned out, had died centuries before their burial.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers a response to the question that opens the text.
It introduces a term that is defined in the sentence that follows.
It describes a method that was used to date the skeletons.
It disputes a claim made in the previous sentence.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: did people in prehistoric Britain preserve their dead? The underlined sentence answers it, reporting that Parker Pearson and his colleagues argue that some did, and the rest of the text gives the evidence. Choice A states this function.

B.why_wrong: No term is introduced, and the next sentence describes the site, not a definition.

C.why_wrong: The sentence names the researchers and their view; the dating evidence comes later in the text.

D.why_wrong: The previous sentence is a question, not a claim, and the underlined sentence answers it rather than disputing it.
